items.caption: One week of milk cartons: what ratio does our cafeteria actually pour?
items.explanation: We counted every carton taken at lunch for five days. Chocolate came to 168 and white came to 96. Written as a ratio that is 168 to 96, and both numbers divide by 24, so the simplest form is 7 to 4. That means for every 7 chocolate cartons the cafeteria puts out, it only needs 4 white ones. The ratio is not a total and it is not a difference. It is a comparison, and it stayed close to 7 to 4 on four of the five days.

items.caption: The biggest bag of dog food was not the better buy
items.explanation: Three bag sizes, three prices. To compare them we had to get every price down to the same unit: dollars for one pound. We divided price by weight each time. The 30 pound bag looked like the deal because the number on the shelf was biggest, but at $1.53 per pound it cost more per pound than the 15 pound bag at $1.39. Unit rate is what makes different sized packages comparable at all.

items.caption: Scaling a family arepa recipe from 4 people to 30
items.explanation: The recipe uses 2 cups of flour for 4 people. We built a table of equivalent ratios instead of guessing: 4 people to 2 cups, 8 to 4, 12 to 6, and so on. Every row multiplies both numbers by the same amount, which is why the plotted points fall on a straight line through the origin. For 30 people the table gives 15 cups. The line let us read off any size, including sizes we never wrote down.

data.title: Flour needed as the guest list grows

items.caption: How our homeroom gets to school, as percents of 25 students
items.explanation: Counting 25 students, 9 walk, 11 ride the bus, 4 are driven, and 1 bikes. To turn each count into a percent we asked what part of 100 it would be, so we scaled the ratio 9 out of 25 up to 36 out of 100. The four percents add to 100, which is the check we used to know we had not lost anyone. Percent is just a ratio with a fixed second number.

data.title: Percent of homeroom by travel method

items.caption: How many three-quarter-cup servings fit in each popcorn tin?
items.explanation: Dividing by a fraction stopped feeling strange once we drew the tins. A 6 cup tin holds 6 divided by three fourths servings. We marked the tin in quarter cups, found 24 quarters, and grouped them by threes to get 8 servings. That is the same answer as multiplying 6 by four thirds. The quotient answers a real question here: how many groups of that size fit, not how much is in one group.

data.title: Servings of three fourths of a cup

items.caption: Spending a forty dollar gift card down to zero, one decimal at a time
items.explanation: Six purchases, all with cents. We kept a running balance and lined up the decimal points every single time, because the place value has to match before you subtract. The balance went 40.00, 33.51, 28.86, 24.11, 12.62, 5.13, 0.64. The last stop was the interesting one: 0.64 left is not enough for anything in the store, so a leftover that small is really a rounding lesson about what money you can actually use.

data.title: Gift card balance after each purchase

items.caption: Our school garden bed is not a rectangle, so we cut it into three shapes
items.explanation: The bed is an L shape with a slanted corner. We decomposed it into one rectangle and two right triangles, found each area separately, then added. The rectangle was 42 square feet, the big triangle 13.5, the small one 4.5, for 60 square feet in total. Decomposing works because area is additive: the pieces do not overlap and nothing is left out. We checked by covering the drawing in one foot squares and counting.

items.caption: Packing a shoebox with half-inch cubes instead of one-inch cubes
items.explanation: The box measures 12 by 6.5 by 4.5 inches. One inch cubes do not fit the half inch edges, so we switched to half inch cubes. Along each edge you get twice as many, so the count multiplies by eight, and each cube is one eighth of a cubic inch. Multiplying the count by the volume of one cube gives 351 cubic inches, the same answer as multiplying the three edge lengths directly. Fractional edges are why counting whole cubes is not enough.

items.caption: Number of siblings in our class, one dot per person
items.explanation: Twenty-six answers on one number line. A dot plot was the right display because the data are small whole numbers and we wanted to see every single response, not a summary. The pile at one and two is obvious, and so is the long thin tail out at five. A histogram would have hidden that tail inside a bin, and a bar graph would have suggested the categories were unrelated instead of being points on a number line.

items.caption: Why we reported the median screen time and not the mean
items.explanation: Fifteen daily totals in minutes. Fourteen of them sit between 35 and 140, and one is 480 because somebody left a tablet playing all day. That single value pulls the mean up to 123 minutes, which describes nobody in the group. The median of 82 minutes sits in the middle of where the data actually are. We reported the median and the interquartile range of 51 minutes, and we said out loud why: the outlier moves the mean and leaves the median alone.

data.title: Two summaries of the same fifteen days

items.caption: Four spots around the Chesapeake, ordered two different ways
items.explanation: The deepest point in the bay is about negative 53 metres and the top of a nearby bridge tower is about positive 116. Ordering by value puts the deepest point first, because negative 53 is less than everything else. Ordering by absolute value puts it third, because 53 metres from sea level is a smaller distance than 116. Those two orders are answering different questions, and mixing them up was the mistake we made first.

items.caption: Every ticket price that still fits a twenty-five dollar budget
items.explanation: Four tickets, twenty-five dollars, so 4p is at most 25 and p is at most 6.25. The answer is not one number. It is every price from zero up to and including 6.25, which is why we graphed it on a number line with a closed circle at 6.25 and shading to the left. The closed circle matters: at exactly 6.25 the total is exactly 25, and that still fits.

data.title: Total cost as ticket price rises
